svg.text: Sea cucumbers live a kilometre down. Squid live in the Falkland Islands.
anyone reading a class's recorded range as its ecological
whether a class is describing itself or one survey's study
a class at 80% one dataset keeps its shape once that dataset
where each class was found in the water column
quartiles and 95th percentile of recorded depth, log scale
Thick bar is the middle half of records, thin line runs to the 95th
percentile, dot is the median. Red is a class whose largest dataset holds more
than half of it — the shape is a study area, not a niche.
each class's records across sea surface temperature, coldest-centred first
°C at the surface · tick is each class's mean
Sorted by mean, because 14 of 16 classes peak in the same 10°C bin
and a modal ordering would tie them. The shapes are the point: squid
is one spike at 5° — the Falklands survey — while corals are
bimodal, peaking at 10° and again at 25°, which is deep-sea corals
and reef corals in one class. Marine mammals are the broadest of all
and the only class with real weight below 0°.
OBIS v3 statistics/env with a taxon filter, fetched 2026-09-18. This is where a class was RECORDED, not where it lives: 88% of all records come from
the top 200 m and a class sampled by divers looks shallow whatever it does. The comparison is between classes, which largely share those biases, never
against the ocean. Reptilia is excluded because OBIS places Aves inside it — 28.2M against Aves' 27.5M, with seabird datasets at the top of both.
